text: Knud Nellemose (12 March 1908, Copenhagen – 14 January 1997, Copenhagen) was a Danish sculptor known for his figures of sportsmen and statues of famous Danes. Between 1927 and 1933, with some interruptions, he studied under Einer Utzon-Frank at the Danish Academy. After starting his career as a sports journalist and newspaper illustrator, he transitioned to sculpture, focusing on boxers, footballers, and athletes, often in motion. Initially influenced by Kai Nielsen, he developed a distinct style characterized by rhythmic movements of arms and legs. He traveled to Greece and Italy, where he was particularly impressed by Donatello, but the dynamic representations he created through accentuated muscle shaping and asymmetrical body positions are entirely his own. One notable pre-war work is Avismanden Leitriz (1935), depicting a newspaperman in the clothes he wore when selling papers in Copenhagen’s streets. Highly productive in both stone and bronze, Nellemose created the Marble Church statues of Søren Kierkegaard (1972) and Bernhard Severin Ingemann (1988), as well as numerous groups of footballers. Among his portraits, some focused on the face and others on half figures, include those of archaeologist Peter Vilhelm Glob (1979) and architect Steen Eiler Rasmussen (1988). During the German occupation of the Second World War, Nellemose was a member of the Frit Danmark resistance group, which led to numerous commissions for war memorials, such as those for Silkeborg (1946) and the 4th of May Dormitory in Aarhus (1953). His Erindring (Remembrance) from 1987 is a powerful depiction of a prisoner from a concentration camp. From 1939, he exhibited as a member of the Decembrist artists, and from 1946 at Den Frie Udstilling. His work was also included in the sculpture event of the art competition at the 1948 Summer Olympics. Knud Nellemose's sister, Karin (1905–1993), was a well-known actress who appeared in many stage productions and films.
